sources.title: Trump unveils his new Super Intelligence Force - TechCrunch
passages: So it’s only natural that Trump’s new task force is named in accordance with this new branding.

The Wall Street Journal reports that Clayton will chair the Super Intelligence Force, effectively making him the new AI/SI czar, with Federal Trade Commission Chair Andrew Ferguson, Undersecretary of War for Research and Engineering Emil Michael, and Office of Personnel Management Director Scott Kupor serving as vice chairs.

“The Super Intelligence Force is tasked with coordinating the effort of the Federal Government to ensure that America continues to lead the World in Super Intelligence, which many say is bigger than the Industrial Revolution, and the Internet, and will protect the interests, and improve the lives, of all Americans,” Trump said in a Sunday morning post on his social network Truth Social.

Since then, Trump signed an executive order seeking to rebrand AI as “super intelligence,” a term seemingly embraced, with some stumbles , by the tech executives who gathered at the White House this week to sign a non-binding safety pledge. (The pledge included an impressive typo .)

Back in September, in response to an AI safety debate that the president has largely dismissed as a hoax created by “Radical Left Dumocrats,” Trump said he would nevertheless form an AI Force and appoint an AI czar (“Only High I.Q. individuals need apply!”).
Anthony Ha is TechCrunch’s weekend editor.
Previously, he worked as a tech reporter at Adweek, a senior editor at VentureBeat, a local government reporter at the Hollister Free Lance, and vice president of content at a VC firm.

extraction.body: US President Donald Trump has announced a “Super Intelligence Force” to coordinate federal efforts on advanced artificial intelligence, with Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton taking charge as the administration’s AI czar.The White House panel will report within 120 days on AI’s risks and opportunities. Trump said it would work to maintain America’s global leadership in the frontier technology while protecting Americans’ interests.Trump announced the force on Truth Social following a White House accord in which leading technology companies pledged to uphold their responsibilities to the public.“The president asked that a group be put together,” Clayton said, adding that “the risk of not being first is high”. PANEL TO REVIEW AI RISKSThe force will review AI risks and systems for reporting breaches, hacks and other incidents, and recommend ways to strengthen the government’s response under existing powers. It will report to Trump and White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles.It will also coordinate federal engagement with consumers, public interest groups, religious organisations, critical infrastructure providers and companies developing superintelligence.Federal Trade Commission Chairman Andrew Ferguson, Under Secretary of War for Research and Engineering Emil Michael and Office of Personnel Management Director Scott Kupor will serve as vice chairs.Members will include Vice President JD Vance, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Wiles. Venture capitalist David Sacks and former Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice will serve as external advisers.Sacks held the AI czar role at the start of Trump’s second term.TRUMP’S PUSH FOR ‘SUPER INTELLIGENCE’Trump described superintelligence as a technology that “many say is bigger than the Industrial Revolution, and the Internet”.He had announced the terminology change at the UN General Assembly, arguing that the word “artificial” made the technology sound fake.“The use of the word artificial intelligence makes it sound fake, and it is not fake. It’s actually amazing,” he said.Following the speech, the State Department’s Bureau of International Organization Affairs directed staff to replace “artificial intelligence” with “super intelligence” in official communications.“We will be using ‘SI’ in all remarks, positions and press elements moving forward,” deputy assistant secretary Michael Drager wrote in an email obtained by The Associated Press.The bureau handles US diplomatic engagement with the UN and other multilateral bodies. It was unclear whether other bureaus or federal agencies had received similar instructions.US representatives later used “SI” at a UN Security Council meeting where technology executives called for checks on AI development.SAFETY CONCERNS GROWThe announcement comes amid growing concern over AI safety, with researchers warning of potentially fatal risks from advanced systems. Democratic and Republican lawmakers have called for greater government action.Trump has favoured limited regulation, arguing that excessive oversight could hamper growth and weaken US competitiveness against China.At an event in Washington on Tuesday, he said he did not want to work with Chinese President Xi Jinping on governing AI, arguing that doing so would make it harder for US companies to build better products than their Chinese rivals.“We’re leading now over China and everyone else, and I want to keep it that way,” Trump said.He also said he had discussed AI with Xi during the Chinese leader’s US visit the previous week, adding that Washington already works with Beijing “in so many ways”.- Ends

According to Trump, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton will lead the task force alongside Chairman of the Federal Trade Commission, Andrew Ferguson, Pentagon Chief Technology Officer Emil Michael and the Director of the Office of Personnel Management, Scott Kupor. The task force is in charge of coordinating the government's engagement with religious organizations, superintelligence providers, consumers and AI companies. Trump said SIF will ensure that America continues to lead the world on AI, which he says, "is bigger than the Industrial Revolution, and the internet, and will protect the interests, and improve the lives, of all Americans.' The team, which is led by Clayton, will report to Trump and the White House Chief of Staff, Susie Wiles. Trump made the announcement on Truth Social this morning, describing that the task force was created in response to his White House Accord on Super Intelligence that he hosted the previous week. The president summoned the world's most powerful tech executives to the White House on Tuesday, where he announced that he would be renaming artificial intelligence to super intelligence in all further government communications. "We’re going to be signing a document today at about 5 o’clock, renaming artificial intelligence, because it’s not artificial, we all agree on that," Trump said, "we're going to be renaming it super intelligence." Trump's full embrace of the use of artificial intelligence comes as Democrats have called for a halt to further developing the technology over fears it will put Americans out of work or at a disadvantage. White House officials have stressed the importance of AI pushing ahead despite those concerns, explaining that American technologists must lead the AI boom to prevent China or other rivals from dominating the space. Earlier the same day, the administration rolled out an AI-powered website, America.gov. The site is designed to help citizens access federal information and services, such as filling out passport applications online and enrolling in Medicaid. 'Anyone who has used Grok or Gemini or ChatGPT will understand instantly how to use America.gov,' Trump said at an event unveiling the new website.

At the meal, Trump and six of the CEOs signed a one-page document titled the “White House Accord on Super Intelligence: Joint Commitment on Frontier Responsibilities.”
Amodei, who dined with Trump on Sunday night, this month called for a deliberate slowdown of AI — after doomsday warnings from his former employee Jacob Coxon sparked Democratic calls for regulation.
“The biggest people in the world signed that, and I signed it as president, and it really is a form of protection… I think it’s morally binding.”

Trump fended off questions about polling showing 71% of Americans think the feds are doing too little to regulate AI and about Microsoft founder Bill Gates’ claim Sunday that AI could cause “a billion deaths” if mismanaged.
Trump said there was nothing to fear because the firms would be “policing each other” and “if something goes wrong, their companies are at stake.”
“It’s almost like a constitution in a way,” Trump told a stunned pack of reporters crowded around him and the group of businessmen on the driveway.
The leaders of Anthropic, Google, Meta, Nvidia, OpenAI and XAI signed alongside Trump.
Huang, whom Trump called a “very handsome guy,” said that AI was essential to economic growth and had created about a million jobs in the US.
Trump said the “extremely friendly” lunch, whose bigwigs included Amazon founder Jeff Bezos, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and Palantir CEO Alex Karp, featured “a lot of commonality.”
“I think the technology has very real risks,” Amodei told reporters alongside Trump outside the West Wing.
“We’re leading, and we’re going to keep it that way,” Trump declared.

The tech giants in attendance included Advanced Micro Devices CEO Lisa Su, who joined the head table as Trump hosted Xi for a state dinner last week, venture capitalist Chamath Palihapitiya, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella, Broadcom CEO Hock Tan and Exiger CEO Brandon Daniels.

extraction.body: See more of our coverage in your search results. WASHINGTON — President Trump called for “tremendous self-regulation” of artificial intelligence Tuesday at a White House lunch with tech billionaires — where they agreed to a “morally binding” set of principles for the technology. Trump hosted nearly two dozen business titans in the East Room before surprising journalists by walking his guests onto the driveway outside the West Wing for a 33-minute impromptu press conference. “There’s a belief that there should be tremendous self-regulation,” Trump said during the lunch as he sat between Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg and Nvidia’s Jensen Huang on his right and XAI’s Elon Musk and Google’s Sundar Pichai to his left. “We automatically have regulation with the Department of Justice, the FBI, all of that. But the self-regulation is very important.” At the meal, Trump and six of the CEOs signed a one-page document titled the “White House Accord on Super Intelligence: Joint Commitment on Frontier Responsibilities.” “It’s almost like a constitution in a way,” Trump told a stunned pack of reporters crowded around him and the group of businessmen on the driveway. “The biggest people in the world signed that, and I signed it as president, and it really is a form of protection… I think it’s morally binding.” The leaders of Anthropic, Google, Meta, Nvidia, OpenAI and XAI signed alongside Trump. The accord commits the firms to “four layers” of safeguards, including establishing internal controls to monitor risks to “cybersecurity, biosecurity, and chemical threats, and to ensure that its models do not hack or access technical systems in unintended ways.” Companies will then designate internal teams to track compliance. External auditors will conduct independent reviews, with a committee of each company’s board of directors in charge of “ensur[ing] any issues identified are remediated.” The six companies “will meet regularly to establish standards and best practices to improve the safety of their systems,” the document says, adding, “Over time, it may make sense to codify these steps into laws or regulations.” Zuckerberg said the agreement would yield “multiple layers of auditing and controls, starting with internal risk review, external auditors and evaluators, and agreeing that we’re going to have all of our boards of directors independently review the reports that come from the auditors.” “The idea isn’t that this is the only thing that we will ever do. It is that this is a start and an accord that the whole industry could come to,” Zuckerberg said. Huang, whom Trump called a “very handsome guy,” said that AI was essential to economic growth and had created about a million jobs in the US. “There’s no conflict between innovation, technology, and safety,” Huang said. “You see behind me just an incredible number of leaders in our industry moving together as one, and we’re going to advance this technology that is so consequential to humanity, so consequential to the future prosperity of our nation. We’re going to do it responsibly and safely.” Pichai, jokingly introduced by the president as a “monster,” said “we are signing up to a set of processes and controls, like we do in other areas like financial controls.” Trump fended off questions about polling showing 71% of Americans think the feds are doing too little to regulate AI and about Microsoft founder Bill Gates’ claim Sunday that AI could cause “a billion deaths” if mismanaged. Trump said there was nothing to fear because the firms would be “policing each other” and “if something goes wrong, their companies are at stake.” Trump said that if he learned of catastrophic threats, “I’d come out here, I’d hold a news conference, and I’d let the world know about it.” Trump hosted the unusual driveway press conference shortly before signing orders renaming the technology as “super intelligence ” — a term he pushed last week at the United Nations and during meetings with Chinese President Xi Jinping. The new terminology will be used in official communications, but there’s no guarantee of wider adoption. WASHINGTON — President Trump called for “tremendous self-regulation” of artificial intelligence Tuesday at a White House lunch with tech billionaires — where they agreed to a “morally binding” set of principles for the technology.
Trump hosted nearly two dozen business titans in the East Room before surprising journalists by walking his guests onto the driveway outside the West Wing for a 33-minute impromptu press conference.

“There’s a belief that there should be tremendous self-regulation,” Trump said during the lunch as he sat between Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg and Nvidia’s Jensen Huang on his right and XAI’s Elon Musk and Google’s Sundar Pichai to his left.
“We automatically have regulation with the Department of Justice, the FBI, all of that. But the self-regulation is very important.”
At the meal, Trump and six of the CEOs signed a one-page document titled the “White House Accord on Super Intelligence: Joint Commitment on Frontier Responsibilities.”
“It’s almost like a constitution in a way,” Trump told a stunned pack of reporters crowded around him and the group of businessmen on the driveway.
“The biggest people in the world signed that, and I signed it as president, and it really is a form of protection… I think it’s morally binding.”
The leaders of Anthropic, Google, Meta, Nvidia, OpenAI and XAI signed alongside Trump.

The accord commits the firms to “four layers” of safeguards, including establishing internal controls to monitor risks to “cybersecurity, biosecurity, and chemical threats, and to ensure that its models do not hack or access technical systems in unintended ways.”

Companies will then designate internal teams to track compliance. External auditors will conduct independent reviews, with a committee of each company’s board of directors in charge of “ensur[ing] any issues identified are remediated.”

The six companies “will meet regularly to establish standards and best practices to improve the safety of their systems,” the document says, adding, “Over time, it may make sense to codify these steps into laws or regulations.”

Zuckerberg said the agreement would yield “multiple layers of auditing and controls, starting with internal risk review, external auditors and evaluators, and agreeing that we’re going to have all of our boards of directors independently review the reports that come from the auditors.”
“The idea isn’t that this is the only thing that we will ever do. It is that this is a start and an accord that the whole industry could come to,” Zuckerberg said.
Huang, whom Trump called a “very handsome guy,” said that AI was essential to economic growth and had created about a million jobs in the US.
“There’s no conflict between innovation, technology, and safety,” Huang said.

“You see behind me just an incredible number of leaders in our industry moving together as one, and we’re going to advance this technology that is so consequential to humanity, so consequential to the future prosperity of our nation. We’re going to do it responsibly and safely.”
Pichai, jokingly introduced by the president as a “monster,” said “we are signing up to a set of processes and controls, like we do in other areas like financial controls.”

Trump fended off questions about polling showing 71% of Americans think the feds are doing too little to regulate AI and about Microsoft founder Bill Gates’ claim Sunday that AI could cause “a billion deaths” if mismanaged.
Trump said there was nothing to fear because the firms would be “policing each other” and “if something goes wrong, their companies are at stake.”
Trump said that if he learned of catastrophic threats, “I’d come out here, I’d hold a news conference, and I’d let the world know about it.”

Trump hosted the unusual driveway press conference shortly before signing orders renaming the technology as “super intelligence ” — a term he pushed last week at the United Nations and during meetings with Chinese President Xi Jinping.
The new terminology will be used in official communications, but there’s no guarantee of wider adoption.
Trump said the “extremely friendly” lunch, whose bigwigs included Amazon founder Jeff Bezos, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and Palantir CEO Alex Karp, featured “a lot of commonality.”

“The job they’ve done is unbelievable. We have a very big lead, and we’re going to keep our lead, and it’s a very positive thing. It’s an amazing industry.”
“We’re leading, and we’re going to keep it that way,” Trump declared.
“It’s not artificial. We all agree on that, and we’re going to be renaming it super intelligence, officially renaming it.”

Trump also said that AI companies would make more of an effort to win over reluctant neighbors of massive new data centers springing up around the country.

sources.title: Trump vows to create ‘AI Force’ and appoint czar amid calls to regulate technology’s development
passages: President Donald Trump said Saturday he plans to create an “AI Force” and name an AI czar as the government faces growing calls to impose guardrails on the rapid development of artificial intelligence.

AI’s meteoric growth has led to major stock market gains and buoyed the manufacturing sector through the construction of data centers — which Trump calls “the golden goose.” Yet fears about the technology’s potential to eliminate jobs and AI data centers’ impact on communities have led to a souring in public sentiment.
Trump’s creation of the Space Force in 2019 marked the first new US military service since 1947.
“We will not in any way hinder or stifle the Growth of this incredible Industry,” Trump said in his post Saturday.

Government has to be regulating this.” Venture capitalist David Sacks served as Trump’s AI and cryptocurrency czar until March, when he stepped down after reaching his time limit as a special government employee.
A White House official also said that AI safety would be “on the agenda” when Trump meets with Xi.

“We are leading China, and the rest of the World, and I intend to keep it that way!” Trump has made clear that he considers outpacing China and preserving AI-driven economic gains a higher priority than addressing growing public concerns.
CNN previously reported that Trump officials were contemplating a meeting with major technology and AI chiefs on the sidelines of the high-stakes summit, though nothing has been finalized.
Trump’s announcement comes as the White House and Congress have faced pressure in recent weeks to enact AI safeguards.

WASHINGTON — President Trump called for “tremendous self-regulation” of artificial intelligence Tuesday at a White House lunch with tech billionaires — where they agreed to a “morally binding” set of principles for the technology. Trump hosted nearly two dozen business titans in the East Room before surprising journalists by walking his guests onto the driveway outside the West Wing for a 33-minute impromptu press conference. “There’s a belief that there should be tremendous self-regulation,” Trump said during the lunch as he sat between Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg and Nvidia’s Jensen Huang on his right and XAI’s Elon Musk and Google’s Sundar Pichai to his left. “We automatically have regulation with the Department of Justice, the FBI, all of that. But the self-regulation is very important.” At the meal, Trump and six of the CEOs signed a one-page document titled the “White House Accord on Super Intelligence: Joint Commitment on Frontier Responsibilities.” “It’s almost like a constitution in a way,” Trump told a stunned pack of reporters crowded around him and the group of businessmen on the driveway. “The biggest people in the world signed that, and I signed it as president, and it really is a form of protection… I think it’s morally binding.” The leaders of Anthropic, Google, Meta, Nvidia, OpenAI and XAI signed alongside Trump. The accord commits the firms to “four layers” of safeguards, including establishing internal controls to monitor risks to “cybersecurity, biosecurity, and chemical threats, and to ensure that its models do not hack or access technical systems in unintended ways.” Companies will then designate internal teams to track compliance. External auditors will conduct independent reviews, with a committee of each company’s board of directors in charge of “ensur[ing] any issues identified are remediated.” The six companies “will meet regularly to establish standards and best practices to improve the safety of their systems,” the document says, adding, “Over time, it may make sense to codify these steps into laws or regulations.” Zuckerberg said the agreement would yield “multiple layers of auditing and controls, starting with internal risk review, external auditors and evaluators, and agreeing that we’re going to have all of our boards of directors independently review the reports that come from the auditors.” “The idea isn’t that this is the only thing that we will ever do. It is that this is a start and an accord that the whole industry could come to,” Zuckerberg said. Huang, whom Trump called a “very handsome guy,” said that AI was essential to economic growth and had created about a million jobs in the US. “There’s no conflict between innovation, technology, and safety,” Huang said. “You see behind me just an incredible number of leaders in our industry moving together as one, and we’re going to advance this technology that is so consequential to humanity, so consequential to the future prosperity of our nation. We’re going to do it responsibly and safely.” Pichai, jokingly introduced by the president as a “monster,” said “we are signing up to a set of processes and controls, like we do in other areas like financial controls.” Trump fended off questions about polling showing 71% of Americans think the feds are doing too little to regulate AI and about Microsoft founder Bill Gates’ claim Sunday that AI could cause “a billion deaths” if mismanaged. Trump said there was nothing to fear because the firms would be “policing each other” and “if something goes wrong, their companies are at stake.” Trump said that if he learned of catastrophic threats, “I’d come out here, I’d hold a news conference, and I’d let the world know about it.” Trump hosted the unusual driveway press conference shortly before signing orders renaming the technology as “super intelligence ” — a term he pushed last week at the United Nations and during meetings with Chinese President Xi Jinping. The new terminology will be used in official communications, but there’s no guarantee of wider adoption. Trump said the “extremely friendly” lunch, whose bigwigs included Amazon founder Jeff Bezos, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and Palantir CEO Alex Karp, featured “a lot of commonality.” Amodei, who dined with Trump on Sunday night, this month called for a deliberate slowdown of AI — after doomsday warnings from his former employee Jacob Coxon sparked Democratic calls for regulation. “I think the technology has very real risks,” Amodei told reporters alongside Trump outside the West Wing. The president basked in the presence of the famous tech pioneers — many of whom were invited to his inauguration last year, despite some of the cohort censoring and deplatforming him following the 2021 Capitol riot. “These are the greatest, the most brilliant people probably in the world,” he said. “The job they’ve done is unbelievable. We have a very big lead, and we’re going to keep our lead, and it’s a very positive thing. It’s an amazing industry.” “We’re leading, and we’re going to keep it that way,” Trump declared. “It’s not artificial. We all agree on that, and we’re going to be renaming it super intelligence, officially renaming it.” Morning Report delivers the latest news, videos, photos and more. Trump also said that AI companies would make more of an effort to win over reluctant neighbors of massive new data centers springing up around the country. “They’re going to do things for the community that will be really financially beneficial and otherwise beneficial,” he said. “The one thing that we all have in common is we love our country, and we love the world, and we want to make sure it’s a safe place. And what we’re talking about today will make it a better place and a much safer place.” The tech giants in attendance included Advanced Micro Devices CEO Lisa Su, who joined the head table as Trump hosted Xi for a state dinner last week, venture capitalist Chamath Palihapitiya, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella, Broadcom CEO Hock Tan and Exiger CEO Brandon Daniels.

At the meal, Trump and six of the CEOs signed a one-page document titled the “White House Accord on Super Intelligence: Joint Commitment on Frontier Responsibilities.”
Amodei, who dined with Trump on Sunday night, this month called for a deliberate slowdown of AI — after doomsday warnings from his former employee Jacob Coxon sparked Democratic calls for regulation.
“The biggest people in the world signed that, and I signed it as president, and it really is a form of protection… I think it’s morally binding.”

Trump fended off questions about polling showing 71% of Americans think the feds are doing too little to regulate AI and about Microsoft founder Bill Gates’ claim Sunday that AI could cause “a billion deaths” if mismanaged.
Trump said there was nothing to fear because the firms would be “policing each other” and “if something goes wrong, their companies are at stake.”
“It’s almost like a constitution in a way,” Trump told a stunned pack of reporters crowded around him and the group of businessmen on the driveway.
The leaders of Anthropic, Google, Meta, Nvidia, OpenAI and XAI signed alongside Trump.
Huang, whom Trump called a “very handsome guy,” said that AI was essential to economic growth and had created about a million jobs in the US.
Trump said the “extremely friendly” lunch, whose bigwigs included Amazon founder Jeff Bezos, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and Palantir CEO Alex Karp, featured “a lot of commonality.”
“I think the technology has very real risks,” Amodei told reporters alongside Trump outside the West Wing.
“We’re leading, and we’re going to keep it that way,” Trump declared.

The tech giants in attendance included Advanced Micro Devices CEO Lisa Su, who joined the head table as Trump hosted Xi for a state dinner last week, venture capitalist Chamath Palihapitiya, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella, Broadcom CEO Hock Tan and Exiger CEO Brandon Daniels.

AI’s meteoric growth has led to major stock market gains and buoyed the manufacturing sector through the construction of data centers — which Trump calls “the golden goose.” Yet fears about the technology’s potential to eliminate jobs and AI data centers’ impact on communities have led to a souring in public sentiment.
Trump’s creation of the Space Force in 2019 marked the first new US military service since 1947.
“We will not in any way hinder or stifle the Growth of this incredible Industry,” Trump said in his post Saturday.

Government has to be regulating this.” Venture capitalist David Sacks served as Trump’s AI and cryptocurrency czar until March, when he stepped down after reaching his time limit as a special government employee.
A White House official also said that AI safety would be “on the agenda” when Trump meets with Xi.

“We are leading China, and the rest of the World, and I intend to keep it that way!” Trump has made clear that he considers outpacing China and preserving AI-driven economic gains a higher priority than addressing growing public concerns.

extraction.body: President Trump on Sunday named Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton as his new "AI czar," adding a different category of intelligence, the "artificial" kind, to the U.S. spy chief's portfolio. In a post on Truth Social , Trump said Clayton will lead a newly formed "Super Intelligence Force" alongside Federal Trade Commission Chair Andrew Ferguson, Under Secretary of Defense for Research and Engineering Emil Michael and Office of Personnel Management Director Scott Kupor. The group will report directly to Trump and White House chief of staff Susie Wiles. Its goal, Trump wrote, is "to ensure that America continues to lead the World in Super Intelligence, which many say is bigger than the Industrial Revolution, and the Internet, and will protect the interests, and improve the lives, of all Americans." Clayton will keep his job as DNI, which oversees the nation's 18 intelligence agencies. Trump's announcement follows meeting last Tuesday at the White House where top AI executives signed what he called a " morally binding " agreement to police themselves in order to prevent their increasingly powerful models from going rogue and harming humanity . "There's a belief that there should be tremendous self-regulation," the president said at the meeting. "This is going to be all for the good, and we're going to have it be nice and safe." Despite new polls showing that 86% of Americans want AI companies to meet independent safety standards even if doing so slows development — with 74% largely mistrusting the leaders of those companies — Trump insisted in recent days that federal regulations are unnecessary and that those who say otherwise are " Conspiracy Theorists, Treasonists, Traitors, and Leakers ." "The only control or 'guardrails' that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades!" he wrote on social media . Elsewhere, Trump has said that regulation would handicap the U.S. in its race to "win" AI. "Whoever wins AI ... that's the group that wins," Trump told the United Nations General Assembly last month . "We're leading now over China by a lot and everyone else, and we're going to keep it that way." According to the Guardian , Trump's previous AI and crypto czar, billionaire tech investor David Sacks, consistently "counseled the president to give a soft touch to AI regulation, helping push executive orders and other measures aimed at loosening restrictions on the technology." Sacks also "maintains direct financial stakes in multiple AI companies," the paper reported, though he took steps to divest some of his holdings last year while serving in the administration. He stepped down in March. Will Clayton follow Sacks's lead? Or will he chart a new course? Here's what we know so far. Clayton, 60, is a registered independent with degrees from the University of Pennsylvania (engineering, law) and the University of Cambridge (economics). As a lawyer in private practice, he focused mostly on Wall Street: mergers and acquisitions, market offerings and regulatory proceedings. During Trump's first term, from 2017 to 2020, Clayton chaired the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission. From March 2021 to April 2025, Clayton served as chair and "lead independent director" of the board of Apollo Global Management . (Apollo has owned a 90% majority stake in Yahoo since September 2021.) In late 2024, Trump nominated Clayton to serve as U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of New York, his first prosecutorial job; Trump later appointed Clayton to serve in an acting capacity after New York Sen. Chuck Schumer blocked his appointment. Reports suggest Clayton was also considered for roles as secretary of the treasury, attorney general and director of the Central Intelligence Agency. In November 2025, Trump ordered the Department of Justice to investigate Democrats associated with Jeffrey Epstein, and U.S. Attorney General Pam Bondi assigned Clayton to lead the probe . After former Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard resigned in May 2026, Trump tapped Clayton to replace her. "He's very qualified," Democratic Sen. Mark Warner of Virginia said at the time . But Clayton sidestepped questions over who won the 2020 election during his July confirmation hearings, and he was confirmed without Democratic support. "I'm not an election denier," Clayton told the Senate. "He went through our processes, and Joe Biden became the president of the United States." During his DNI confirmation hearings, Clayton described AI as "a game changer ," warning that it represents "not only an opportunity but a threat." "We should just all recognize that," he continued. "When something is both an opportunity and a threat, you better get your arms around it." On Tuesday, Clayton attended Trump's White House meeting with top AI executives. Speaking afterward to CNBC, he used the president's new preferred term for AI — i.e., "superintelligence " — while pushing back against lawmakers who have called for regulating or pausing U.S. AI development. "Super intelligence is a national security issue, and that was something that was recognized yesterday by not just the industry leaders but everybody in the room," Clayton said. "But to, in some way, not try to drive forward inside the United States, with companies that are regulated in the United States ... to somehow say we should back away from this and let the rest of the world develop these models and implement these models? I don't think anybody in that room, and I don't think any American, should think that that's a good strategy." Asked to respond to criticism from Democratic Sen. Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts that Trump's current policy of letting AI companies police themselves will prove to be "a recipe for disaster," Clayton suggested that the U.S. government's existing regulatory framework could also help keep AI in check. "My response to the American people on that front is we have a Federal Trade Commission, we have a Department of Justice," Clayton said. "I know the leaders of both those organizations, and they're committed to protecting the American people in this regard." According to Trump's post, the Super Intelligence Force will coordinate the federal government's dealings with AI companies, infrastructure providers, consumers, public interest groups and religious organizations, CNN reported . Last month, Trump wrote on social media that he would "be announcing, in the near future, the AI 'Czar.' "Only High I.Q. individuals need apply!" he added. In the same post, the president again dismissed concerns about AI safety as a "hoax" perpetrated by "Radical Left Democrats." He also wrote that going forward, his administration would not "in any way hinder or stifle the Growth of this incredible Industry," which he described as "the next Industrial Revolution, or Internet" — only "even larger and more impactful." "Rather, we will cherish it, help it, and watch over it, as it grows!" Trump explained. As for reining in "bad" actors, he wrote, "we can do that, very easily, with our already existing Criminal and Civil Justice System." Clayton, it seems, will now be in charge of cherishing, helping and watching over the AI industry as it grows. He's "a good man," Trump told Axios when the outlet asked last week if Clayton was being considered for the job . "He's right here. That's a good idea." It's unclear what happened to a separate idea Trump floated last month, which he called "the AI Force." "I am forming the AI Force, much like I did Space Force , which has been a tremendous SUCCESS, in my First Term," Trump wrote in his September social media post about naming an AI czar. According to Axios , Trump's AI Force idea "caught advisers by surprise," setting off "a mad dash" within the administration "to imagine what AI Force would look like." When Sacks served as AI czar, he repeatedly persuaded the president and his administration to resist new AI restrictions, including state laws to limit AI . Since leaving the White House, Sacks has "maintained close ties with the president," according to the Guardian, and "in May, he successfully urged Trump to scrap an executive order that would've subjected AI models to government review." The Wall Street Journal recently reported the Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and White House chief of staff Susie Wiles were "caught off guard and unhappy" with Trump's decision after they "spent months negotiating to increase oversight of AI and had consulted a range of industry executives on the order." According to the Journal's sources, Wiles "told others that Sacks had persuaded Trump" to back down "in a last-minute call," leaving Bessent "worried that AI-led cyberattacks could wreak havoc on the nation's banking system."

passages: Donald Trump on Sunday named Jay Clayton, the director of national intelligence , to serve also as the new White House AI czar.
Trump had initially created the AI and cryptocurrency czar position when he returned to the White House in January 2025.
Trump previously floated Clayton’s name as a potential AI czar, telling Axios in September that Clayton is ‘“a good man” and the prospect of appointing him was “a good idea”.
In a social media post on Sunday, Trump announced that Clayton would lead what the US president called “the Super Intelligence Force (SIF)”.
Clayton, who leads the US’s 18 intelligence agencies , previously served as the top federal prosecutor in Manhattan and led the Securities and Exchange Commission during Trump’s first term.
In September, Trump announced he was creating an “AI Force” and a czar to oversee the technology’s growth and monitor for “bad” development.
The announcement came after tech industry leaders warned that AI was developing too rapidly to control and that it could harm humans.

Trump’s post also said the SIF would “coordinate the federal government’s engagement with consumers, public interest groups, religious organizations, critical infrastructure providers, and super intelligence companies”.
But to address concerns, the president created an advisory committee in addition to the czar – who he previously promised would be led by a “High IQ” individual.
Trump also recently met with AI industry leaders to discuss concerns.
Trump has insisted continued development is paramount to defeating China in the global AI race.

passages: US President Donald Trump has appointed Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton as the administration's AI czar, the Wall Street Journal reported on Saturday, citing an interview with Clayton.
Clayton, who was appointed intelligence chief in August, will lead a new White House panel tasked with reporting within 120 days on the risks and opportunities posed by AI, the newspaper said.

Clayton's panel will review AI-related risks and current government reporting mechanisms for breaches, hacks and other incidents, and recommend ways to strengthen federal-response capabilities under existing authorities, the Journal said, citing the task force's charter.
Venture capitalist David Sacks held the AI czar role at the beginning of Trump's second term.
Trump has appeared to take a light touch toward AI regulation, arguing that excessive oversight could weaken competitiveness against China.
He said on Tuesday that he does not want to work with Chinese President Xi Jinping on governing AI technology.

extraction.body: President Trump on Sunday named Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton as his new "AI czar," adding a different category of intelligence, the "artificial" kind, to the U.S. spy chief's portfolio. In a post on Truth Social , Trump said Clayton will lead a newly formed "Super Intelligence Force" alongside Federal Trade Commission Chair Andrew Ferguson, Under Secretary of Defense for Research and Engineering Emil Michael and Office of Personnel Management Director Scott Kupor. The group will report directly to Trump and White House chief of staff Susie Wiles. Its goal, Trump wrote, is "to ensure that America continues to lead the World in Super Intelligence, which many say is bigger than the Industrial Revolution, and the Internet, and will protect the interests, and improve the lives, of all Americans." Clayton will keep his job as DNI, which oversees the nation's 18 intelligence agencies. Trump's announcement follows meeting last Tuesday at the White House where top AI executives signed what he called a " morally binding " agreement to police themselves in order to prevent their increasingly powerful models from going rogue and harming humanity . "There's a belief that there should be tremendous self-regulation," the president said at the meeting. "This is going to be all for the good, and we're going to have it be nice and safe." Despite new polls showing that 86% of Americans want AI companies to meet independent safety standards even if doing so slows development — with 74% largely mistrusting the leaders of those companies — Trump insisted in recent days that federal regulations are unnecessary and that those who say otherwise are " Conspiracy Theorists, Treasonists, Traitors, and Leakers ." "The only control or 'guardrails' that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades!" he wrote on social media . Elsewhere, Trump has said that regulation would handicap the U.S. in its race to "win" AI. "Whoever wins AI ... that's the group that wins," Trump told the United Nations General Assembly last month . "We're leading now over China by a lot and everyone else, and we're going to keep it that way." According to the Guardian , Trump's previous AI and crypto czar, billionaire tech investor David Sacks, consistently "counseled the president to give a soft touch to AI regulation, helping push executive orders and other measures aimed at loosening restrictions on the technology." Sacks also "maintains direct financial stakes in multiple AI companies," the paper reported, though he took steps to divest some of his holdings last year while serving in the administration. He stepped down in March. Will Clayton follow Sacks's lead? Or will he chart a new course? Here's what we know so far. Clayton, 60, is a registered independent with degrees from the University of Pennsylvania (engineering, law) and the University of Cambridge (economics). As a lawyer in private practice, he focused mostly on Wall Street: mergers and acquisitions, market offerings and regulatory proceedings. During Trump's first term, from 2017 to 2020, Clayton chaired the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission. From March 2021 to April 2025, Clayton served as chair and "lead independent director" of the board of Apollo Global Management . (Apollo has owned a 90% majority stake in Yahoo since September 2021.) In late 2024, Trump nominated Clayton to serve as U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of New York, his first prosecutorial job; Trump later appointed Clayton to serve in an acting capacity after New York Sen. Chuck Schumer blocked his appointment. Reports suggest Clayton was also considered for roles as secretary of the treasury, attorney general and director of the Central Intelligence Agency. In November 2025, Trump ordered the Department of Justice to investigate Democrats associated with Jeffrey Epstein, and U.S. Attorney General Pam Bondi assigned Clayton to lead the probe . After former Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard resigned in May 2026, Trump tapped Clayton to replace her. "He's very qualified," Democratic Sen. Mark Warner of Virginia said at the time . But Clayton sidestepped questions over who won the 2020 election during his July confirmation hearings, and he was confirmed without Democratic support. "I'm not an election denier," Clayton told the Senate. "He went through our processes, and Joe Biden became the president of the United States." During his DNI confirmation hearings, Clayton described AI as "a game changer ," warning that it represents "not only an opportunity but a threat." "We should just all recognize that," he continued. "When something is both an opportunity and a threat, you better get your arms around it." On Tuesday, Clayton attended Trump's White House meeting with top AI executives. Speaking afterward to CNBC, he used the president's new preferred term for AI — i.e., "superintelligence " — while pushing back against lawmakers who have called for regulating or pausing U.S. AI development. "Super intelligence is a national security issue, and that was something that was recognized yesterday by not just the industry leaders but everybody in the room," Clayton said. "But to, in some way, not try to drive forward inside the United States, with companies that are regulated in the United States ... to somehow say we should back away from this and let the rest of the world develop these models and implement these models? I don't think anybody in that room, and I don't think any American, should think that that's a good strategy." Asked to respond to criticism from Democratic Sen. Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts that Trump's current policy of letting AI companies police themselves will prove to be "a recipe for disaster," Clayton suggested that the U.S. government's existing regulatory framework could also help keep AI in check. "My response to the American people on that front is we have a Federal Trade Commission, we have a Department of Justice," Clayton said. "I know the leaders of both those organizations, and they're committed to protecting the American people in this regard." According to Trump's post, the Super Intelligence Force will coordinate the federal government's dealings with AI companies, infrastructure providers, consumers, public interest groups and religious organizations, CNN reported . Last month, Trump wrote on social media that he would "be announcing, in the near future, the AI 'Czar.' "Only High I.Q. individuals need apply!" he added. In the same post, the president again dismissed concerns about AI safety as a "hoax" perpetrated by "Radical Left Democrats." He also wrote that going forward, his administration would not "in any way hinder or stifle the Growth of this incredible Industry," which he described as "the next Industrial Revolution, or Internet" — only "even larger and more impactful." "Rather, we will cherish it, help it, and watch over it, as it grows!" Trump explained. As for reining in "bad" actors, he wrote, "we can do that, very easily, with our already existing Criminal and Civil Justice System." Clayton, it seems, will now be in charge of cherishing, helping and watching over the AI industry as it grows. He's "a good man," Trump told Axios when the outlet asked last week if Clayton was being considered for the job . "He's right here. That's a good idea." It's unclear what happened to a separate idea Trump floated last month, which he called "the AI Force." "I am forming the AI Force, much like I did Space Force , which has been a tremendous SUCCESS, in my First Term," Trump wrote in his September social media post about naming an AI czar. According to Axios , Trump's AI Force idea "caught advisers by surprise," setting off "a mad dash" within the administration "to imagine what AI Force would look like." When Sacks served as AI czar, he repeatedly persuaded the president and his administration to resist new AI restrictions, including state laws to limit AI . Since leaving the White House, Sacks has "maintained close ties with the president," according to the Guardian, and "in May, he successfully urged Trump to scrap an executive order that would've subjected AI models to government review." The Wall Street Journal recently reported the Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and White House chief of staff Susie Wiles were "caught off guard and unhappy" with Trump's decision after they "spent months negotiating to increase oversight of AI and had consulted a range of industry executives on the order." According to the Journal's sources, Wiles "told others that Sacks had persuaded Trump" to back down "in a last-minute call," leaving Bessent "worried that AI-led cyberattacks could wreak havoc on the nation's banking system."

Sacks also "maintains direct financial stakes in multiple AI companies," the paper reported, though he took steps to divest some of his holdings last year while serving in the administration. He stepped down in March.
Will Clayton follow Sacks's lead? Or will he chart a new course? Here's what we know so far.

Clayton, 60, is a registered independent with degrees from the University of Pennsylvania (engineering, law) and the University of Cambridge (economics). As a lawyer in private practice, he focused mostly on Wall Street: mergers and acquisitions, market offerings and regulatory proceedings. During Trump's first term, from 2017 to 2020, Clayton chaired the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission. From March 2021 to April 2025, Clayton served as chair and "lead independent director" of the board of Apollo Global Management . (Apollo has owned a 90% majority stake in Yahoo since September 2021.)

In late 2024, Trump nominated Clayton to serve as U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of New York, his first prosecutorial job; Trump later appointed Clayton to serve in an acting capacity after New York Sen. Chuck Schumer blocked his appointment. Reports suggest Clayton was also considered for roles as secretary of the treasury, attorney general and director of the Central Intelligence Agency. In November 2025, Trump ordered the Department of Justice to investigate Democrats associated with Jeffrey Epstein, and U.S. Attorney General Pam Bondi assigned Clayton to lead the probe .

After former Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard resigned in May 2026, Trump tapped Clayton to replace her. "He's very qualified," Democratic Sen. Mark Warner of Virginia said at the time . But Clayton sidestepped questions over who won the 2020 election during his July confirmation hearings, and he was confirmed without Democratic support.
"I'm not an election denier," Clayton told the Senate. "He went through our processes, and Joe Biden became the president of the United States."
During his DNI confirmation hearings, Clayton described AI as "a game changer ," warning that it represents "not only an opportunity but a threat."
"We should just all recognize that," he continued. "When something is both an opportunity and a threat, you better get your arms around it."

On Tuesday, Clayton attended Trump's White House meeting with top AI executives. Speaking afterward to CNBC, he used the president's new preferred term for AI — i.e., "superintelligence " — while pushing back against lawmakers who have called for regulating or pausing U.S. AI development.

"Super intelligence is a national security issue, and that was something that was recognized yesterday by not just the industry leaders but everybody in the room," Clayton said. "But to, in some way, not try to drive forward inside the United States, with companies that are regulated in the United States ... to somehow say we should back away from this and let the rest of the world develop these models and implement these models? I don't think anybody in that room, and I don't think any American, should think that that's a good strategy."

Asked to respond to criticism from Democratic Sen. Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts that Trump's current policy of letting AI companies police themselves will prove to be "a recipe for disaster," Clayton suggested that the U.S. government's existing regulatory framework could also help keep AI in check.

"My response to the American people on that front is we have a Federal Trade Commission, we have a Department of Justice," Clayton said. "I know the leaders of both those organizations, and they're committed to protecting the American people in this regard."

According to Trump's post, the Super Intelligence Force will coordinate the federal government's dealings with AI companies, infrastructure providers, consumers, public interest groups and religious organizations, CNN reported .
Last month, Trump wrote on social media that he would "be announcing, in the near future, the AI 'Czar.'
"Only High I.Q. individuals need apply!" he added.

In the same post, the president again dismissed concerns about AI safety as a "hoax" perpetrated by "Radical Left Democrats." He also wrote that going forward, his administration would not "in any way hinder or stifle the Growth of this incredible Industry," which he described as "the next Industrial Revolution, or Internet" — only "even larger and more impactful."

"Rather, we will cherish it, help it, and watch over it, as it grows!" Trump explained. As for reining in "bad" actors, he wrote, "we can do that, very easily, with our already existing Criminal and Civil Justice System."

Clayton, it seems, will now be in charge of cherishing, helping and watching over the AI industry as it grows. He's "a good man," Trump told Axios when the outlet asked last week if Clayton was being considered for the job . "He's right here. That's a good idea."
It's unclear what happened to a separate idea Trump floated last month, which he called "the AI Force."
"I am forming the AI Force, much like I did Space Force , which has been a tremendous SUCCESS, in my First Term," Trump wrote in his September social media post about naming an AI czar.
According to Axios , Trump's AI Force idea "caught advisers by surprise," setting off "a mad dash" within the administration "to imagine what AI Force would look like."

When Sacks served as AI czar, he repeatedly persuaded the president and his administration to resist new AI restrictions, including state laws to limit AI . Since leaving the White House, Sacks has "maintained close ties with the president," according to the Guardian, and "in May, he successfully urged Trump to scrap an executive order that would've subjected AI models to government review."

The Wall Street Journal recently reported the Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and White House chief of staff Susie Wiles were "caught off guard and unhappy" with Trump's decision after they "spent months negotiating to increase oversight of AI and had consulted a range of industry executives on the order." According to the Journal's sources, Wiles "told others that Sacks had persuaded Trump" to back down "in a last-minute call," leaving Bessent "worried that AI-led cyberattacks could wreak havoc on the nation's banking system."

passages: Donald Trump on Sunday named Jay Clayton, the director of national intelligence , to serve also as the new White House AI czar.
Trump had initially created the AI and cryptocurrency czar position when he returned to the White House in January 2025.
Trump previously floated Clayton’s name as a potential AI czar, telling Axios in September that Clayton is ‘“a good man” and the prospect of appointing him was “a good idea”.
In a social media post on Sunday, Trump announced that Clayton would lead what the US president called “the Super Intelligence Force (SIF)”.
Clayton, who leads the US’s 18 intelligence agencies , previously served as the top federal prosecutor in Manhattan and led the Securities and Exchange Commission during Trump’s first term.
In September, Trump announced he was creating an “AI Force” and a czar to oversee the technology’s growth and monitor for “bad” development.
The announcement came after tech industry leaders warned that AI was developing too rapidly to control and that it could harm humans.

Trump’s post also said the SIF would “coordinate the federal government’s engagement with consumers, public interest groups, religious organizations, critical infrastructure providers, and super intelligence companies”.
But to address concerns, the president created an advisory committee in addition to the czar – who he previously promised would be led by a “High IQ” individual.
Trump also recently met with AI industry leaders to discuss concerns.
Trump has insisted continued development is paramount to defeating China in the global AI race.

passages: US President Donald Trump has appointed Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton as the administration's AI czar, the Wall Street Journal reported on Saturday, citing an interview with Clayton.
Clayton, who was appointed intelligence chief in August, will lead a new White House panel tasked with reporting within 120 days on the risks and opportunities posed by AI, the newspaper said.

Clayton's panel will review AI-related risks and current government reporting mechanisms for breaches, hacks and other incidents, and recommend ways to strengthen federal-response capabilities under existing authorities, the Journal said, citing the task force's charter.
Venture capitalist David Sacks held the AI czar role at the beginning of Trump's second term.
Trump has appeared to take a light touch toward AI regulation, arguing that excessive oversight could weaken competitiveness against China.
He said on Tuesday that he does not want to work with Chinese President Xi Jinping on governing AI technology.

"The president asked that a group be put together," which the administration refers to as the "Super Intelligence Force," to ensure the US remains a leader in advanced AI while protecting Americans' interests, Clayton told the Journal, adding that "the risk of not being first is high." The safety of AI has become a major issue in recent weeks, with some researchers warning that people building the technology believe it could kill humans within a decade. Several Democratic and Republican lawmakers have responded with alarm and calls for more action. Clayton's panel will review AI-related risks and current government reporting mechanisms for breaches, hacks and other incidents, and recommend ways to strengthen federal-response capabilities under existing authorities, the Journal said, citing the task force's charter. This is the second time Trump has named an adviser to oversee AI-related decisions across the administration. Venture capitalist David Sacks held the AI czar role at the beginning of Trump's second term. The task force's vice chairs will be Emil Michael, Scott Kupor and Federal Trade Commission Chair Andrew Ferguson, while members will include Vice President JD Vance, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles, according to the report. External advisers will also include Sacks and former Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice, the Journal said. passages: Tether relaunches its $184 billion USDT on Bitcoin in October 2026, 12 years after abandoning it for faster, cheaper networks like Tron and Ethereum.
This new integration will connect Bitcoin, the oldest blockchain, directly with USDT, the largest stablecoin valued at around $184 billion, designed to maintain a value of $1.
Tether CEO Paolo Ardoino captured the sentiment of this return with the phrase, "It's coming home." But does this move mean that Bitcoin will become a payments network again?
So far, Tether has not disclosed any exchanges or payment companies that plan to support the Bitcoin version.
El Salvador illustrates the struggle Bitcoin has faced as a payment method.
Although the country adopted Bitcoin as legal tender in 2021, a University of Central America survey revealed that 92% of Salvadorans reported not using it in 2024.
Recently, on September 29, the government announced plans for a stablecoin platform called Sivar on Coinbase's Base network, rather than building it on Bitcoin.
Additionally, El Salvador has opted for another blockchain for its stablecoin initiatives.
As a result, this relaunch primarily benefits Tether by reaching new users, while Bitcoin holders see minimal short-term change in BTC price or miner income.
This time, Utexo—a company backed by Tether with a license to distribute USDT under Tether's brand through exchanges, wallets, and payment providers —will issue USDT.
Bitcoin holders might find the launch less beneficial than it appears at first glance.

A USDT balance on Bitcoin represents a dollar claim on Tether, meaning it offers no exposure to Bitcoin's price fluctuations, and the limits and rules governing Bitcoin's 21 million coins remain unchanged.
As with XRP, increased network activity does not automatically increase demand for BTC.
Tether provides regular updates on how much USDT it has issued on each network, making it easy to track progress.

If major exchanges begin to support Bitcoin-based USDT and its supply increases steadily through March 2027, particularly with Lightning support in place, Bitcoin could reclaim a portion of the payments landscape.
Utexo builds on the RGB protocol, which enables tokens to operate on Bitcoin while keeping most transaction details private off the public ledger.
This design enables private transfers, direct exchanges between BTC and USDT, and Bitcoin-backed loans without creating additional tokens.
Utexo also plans to integrate USDT into the Lightning Network, Bitcoin's faster payment layer.

Furthermore, Bitcoin's inherent design can hinder heavy payment traffic.

It adds a new block about every 10 minutes, which simplifies verification but limits the number of transactions it can process—leading to higher fees and longer wait times during periods of high demand.
They generate new coins alongside transaction fees for recording each transaction.
However, as the reward for mining new coins halves roughly every four years, fees need to pay for Bitcoin's security over time.
The privacy aspect could spark more interest than potential fees.

sources.title: Visa, Mastercard, Stripe, and Coinbase Commit $1 Billion to New Stablecoin: Is Open USD a Challenge to Tether, USDC, and RLUSD? - aol.com
passages: Visa, Mastercard, Stripe, Coinbase, and Shopify committed $1 billion to Open USD, launched September 30 against Tether's $184 billion market cap.
A stablecoin is designed to maintain a value of $1, and with major payment companies backing it, OUSD is entering the market with significant support.
The $1 billion represents liquidity that these partners are ready to provide, allowing users to easily convert OUSD into dollars.
While this commitment is substantial, it still pales in comparison to the existing market giants.
This raises the question: Does Open USD pose a threat to Tether (CRYPTO: USDT), USD Coin (CRYPTO: USDC), and Ripple's RLUSD (CRYPTO: RLUSD)?
The clearest sign of Open USD's impact will be how it is used for settlements.

If Visa, Mastercard, or Stripe start processing payments in OUSD by default, or if OUSD's supply grows into the tens of billions by mid-2027, the competitive landscape for all three established stablecoins could shift dramatically.
OUSD’s profit-sharing structure could incentivize Coinbase, Visa, and other partners to favor it over USDC, potentially pulling more business away from Circle.
OUSD is significantly smaller than established players.
Adding pressure is Visa's involvement; the company has been working on settlement programs using USDC, while it now supports a rival that shares its revenue.
So far, Visa, Mastercard, and Stripe have not committed to using OUSD for default merchant or card transactions, yet doing so could significantly boost its usage.
The company Bridge, acquired by Stripe for $1.1 billion in 2024, issues OUSD and provides monthly updates on its reserves.
BlackRock, Lead Bank, and BNY Mellon manage these reserves.
The organization behind OUSD, Open Standard, reports that its partner network has grown to over 200 companies, up from 140 in June.
Ripple sells RLUSD to banks and payment institutions for cross-border transactions, just the type of customers that OUSD’s partners are already accommodating.
With OUSD backed by major players like Visa and Mastercard, institutions assessing payment networks will have to consider this strong competitor.
Among established tokens, USDC faces the biggest risk from Open USD.
Circle already splits reserve income with its distributors, and since Coinbase benefits from USDC revenue and is also an OUSD partner, it can promote whichever token offers them more profit.
Unlike Tether and Circle, which issue USDC and keep most of the interest income from their reserves, OUSD shares most of that revenue with its partners.
These partners receive earnings based on their participation, and they can create and redeem tokens at $1 without any fees.
This existing habit helped them establish extensive markets that a new entrant cannot replicate overnight.
However, OUSD is starting within the financial systems that handle payments directly, leveraging card networks and Shopify stores, where USDT and USDC have minimal influence.
This market includes many of the 35% of Americans who now own cryptocurrency.
As Open Standard CEO Zach Abrams explains, "Every other stablecoin is building a fund.
For XRP holders (CRYPTO:XRP), the fate of RLUSD primarily relates to Ripple's business developments and does not directly influence XRP’s value.

Tether is set to relaunch its USDT ( CRYPTO: USDT ) stablecoin on the Bitcoin ( CRYPTO: BTC ) network in October 2026, marking a return 12 years after its initial launch. This new integration will connect Bitcoin, the oldest blockchain, directly with USDT, the largest stablecoin valued at around $184 billion, designed to maintain a value of $1.

In previous years, USDT shifted away from Bitcoin to take advantage of faster and cheaper networks, predominantly operating on platforms like Tron and Ethereum. Tether CEO Paolo Ardoino captured the sentiment of this return with the phrase, “It’s coming home.” But does this move mean that Bitcoin will become a payments network again?

Tether originally launched USDT on Bitcoin in 2014 using the Omni protocol, which recorded tokens on the Bitcoin blockchain. This time, Utexo—a company backed by Tether with a license to distribute USDT under Tether’s brand through exchanges, wallets, and payment providers —will issue USDT.

Utexo builds on the RGB protocol, which enables tokens to operate on Bitcoin while keeping most transaction details private off the public ledger. This design enables private transfers, direct exchanges between BTC and USDT, and Bitcoin-backed loans without creating additional tokens. Utexo also plans to integrate USDT into the Lightning Network, Bitcoin’s faster payment layer.

Bitcoin holders might find the launch less beneficial than it appears at first glance. A USDT balance on Bitcoin represents a dollar claim on Tether, meaning it offers no exposure to Bitcoin’s price fluctuations, and the limits and rules governing Bitcoin’s 21 million coins remain unchanged. As with XRP , increased network activity does not automatically increase demand for BTC.

Miners may also earn less than expected. They generate new coins alongside transaction fees for recording each transaction. However, as the reward for mining new coins halves roughly every four years, fees need to pay for Bitcoin’s security over time. The RGB protocol keeps most transfer data off Bitcoin’s main chain, resulting in significantly lower fee revenue from USDT transactions than from full on-chain transfers.

The privacy aspect could spark more interest than potential fees. Researchers have already suggested integrating shielded Bitcoin using Zcash’s privacy technology, and private dollar transfers on Bitcoin could appeal to businesses that don’t want every transaction visible on a public ledger.

Competition poses a significant obstacle to Bitcoin’s resurgence as a payments network. For years, exchanges, wallets, and payment apps have handled USDT deposits and withdrawals primarily on Tron and Ethereum, where transfers are faster and cheaper. So far, Tether has not disclosed any exchanges or payment companies that plan to support the Bitcoin version.

Furthermore, Bitcoin’s inherent design can hinder heavy payment traffic. It adds a new block about every 10 minutes, which simplifies verification but limits the number of transactions it can process—leading to higher fees and longer wait times during periods of high demand. The Lightning Network was created to address this issue, so Utexo’s plan to add USDT to the Lightning Network will be crucial to its success.

El Salvador illustrates the struggle Bitcoin has faced as a payment method. Although the country adopted Bitcoin as legal tender in 2021, a University of Central America survey revealed that 92% of Salvadorans reported not using it in 2024. Recently, on September 29, the government announced plans for a stablecoin platform called Sivar on Coinbase’s Base network, rather than building it on Bitcoin.

Not with this launch alone. While USDT on Bitcoin offers a dollar-backed token for payments, private transfers, and swaps, Tron and Ethereum still hold most USDT. Additionally, El Salvador has opted for another blockchain for its stablecoin initiatives. As a result, this relaunch primarily benefits Tether by reaching new users, while Bitcoin holders see minimal short-term change in BTC price o r miner income .

Tether provides regular updates on how much USDT it has issued on each network, making it easy to track progress. If major exchanges begin to support Bitcoin-based USDT and its supply increases steadily through March 2027, particularly with Lightning support in place, Bitcoin could reclaim a portion of the payments landscape.

On the other hand, if USDT’s supply on Bitcoin remains relatively small compared to Tron and Ethereum, this relaunch might simply add another token to the mix without significantly increasing payment activity on Bitcoin.

Visa, Mastercard, Stripe, Coinbase, and Shopify committed $1 billion to Open USD, launched September 30 against Tether's $184 billion market cap.
A stablecoin is designed to maintain a value of $1, and with major payment companies backing it, OUSD is entering the market with significant support.
The $1 billion represents liquidity that these partners are ready to provide, allowing users to easily convert OUSD into dollars.
While this commitment is substantial, it still pales in comparison to the existing market giants.
This raises the question: Does Open USD pose a threat to Tether (CRYPTO: USDT), USD Coin (CRYPTO: USDC), and Ripple's RLUSD (CRYPTO: RLUSD)?
The clearest sign of Open USD's impact will be how it is used for settlements.

If Visa, Mastercard, or Stripe start processing payments in OUSD by default, or if OUSD's supply grows into the tens of billions by mid-2027, the competitive landscape for all three established stablecoins could shift dramatically.
OUSD’s profit-sharing structure could incentivize Coinbase, Visa, and other partners to favor it over USDC, potentially pulling more business away from Circle.
OUSD is significantly smaller than established players.
Adding pressure is Visa's involvement; the company has been working on settlement programs using USDC, while it now supports a rival that shares its revenue.
So far, Visa, Mastercard, and Stripe have not committed to using OUSD for default merchant or card transactions, yet doing so could significantly boost its usage.
The company Bridge, acquired by Stripe for $1.1 billion in 2024, issues OUSD and provides monthly updates on its reserves.
BlackRock, Lead Bank, and BNY Mellon manage these reserves.
The organization behind OUSD, Open Standard, reports that its partner network has grown to over 200 companies, up from 140 in June.
Ripple sells RLUSD to banks and payment institutions for cross-border transactions, just the type of customers that OUSD’s partners are already accommodating.
With OUSD backed by major players like Visa and Mastercard, institutions assessing payment networks will have to consider this strong competitor.
Among established tokens, USDC faces the biggest risk from Open USD.
Circle already splits reserve income with its distributors, and since Coinbase benefits from USDC revenue and is also an OUSD partner, it can promote whichever token offers them more profit.
Unlike Tether and Circle, which issue USDC and keep most of the interest income from their reserves, OUSD shares most of that revenue with its partners.
These partners receive earnings based on their participation, and they can create and redeem tokens at $1 without any fees.
This existing habit helped them establish extensive markets that a new entrant cannot replicate overnight.
However, OUSD is starting within the financial systems that handle payments directly, leveraging card networks and Shopify stores, where USDT and USDC have minimal influence.
This market includes many of the 35% of Americans who now own cryptocurrency.
As Open Standard CEO Zach Abrams explains, "Every other stablecoin is building a fund.

sources.title: Visa, Mastercard, Stripe, and Coinbase Commit $1 Billion to New Stablecoin: Is Open USD a Challenge to Tether, USDC, and RLUSD? - aol.com
passages: Visa, Mastercard, Stripe, Coinbase, and Shopify committed $1 billion to Open USD, launched September 30 against Tether's $184 billion market cap.
A stablecoin is designed to maintain a value of $1, and with major payment companies backing it, OUSD is entering the market with significant support.
The $1 billion represents liquidity that these partners are ready to provide, allowing users to easily convert OUSD into dollars.
While this commitment is substantial, it still pales in comparison to the existing market giants.
This raises the question: Does Open USD pose a threat to Tether (CRYPTO: USDT), USD Coin (CRYPTO: USDC), and Ripple's RLUSD (CRYPTO: RLUSD)?
The clearest sign of Open USD's impact will be how it is used for settlements.

If Visa, Mastercard, or Stripe start processing payments in OUSD by default, or if OUSD's supply grows into the tens of billions by mid-2027, the competitive landscape for all three established stablecoins could shift dramatically.
OUSD’s profit-sharing structure could incentivize Coinbase, Visa, and other partners to favor it over USDC, potentially pulling more business away from Circle.
OUSD is significantly smaller than established players.
Adding pressure is Visa's involvement; the company has been working on settlement programs using USDC, while it now supports a rival that shares its revenue.
So far, Visa, Mastercard, and Stripe have not committed to using OUSD for default merchant or card transactions, yet doing so could significantly boost its usage.
The company Bridge, acquired by Stripe for $1.1 billion in 2024, issues OUSD and provides monthly updates on its reserves.
BlackRock, Lead Bank, and BNY Mellon manage these reserves.
The organization behind OUSD, Open Standard, reports that its partner network has grown to over 200 companies, up from 140 in June.
Ripple sells RLUSD to banks and payment institutions for cross-border transactions, just the type of customers that OUSD’s partners are already accommodating.
With OUSD backed by major players like Visa and Mastercard, institutions assessing payment networks will have to consider this strong competitor.
Among established tokens, USDC faces the biggest risk from Open USD.
Circle already splits reserve income with its distributors, and since Coinbase benefits from USDC revenue and is also an OUSD partner, it can promote whichever token offers them more profit.
Unlike Tether and Circle, which issue USDC and keep most of the interest income from their reserves, OUSD shares most of that revenue with its partners.
These partners receive earnings based on their participation, and they can create and redeem tokens at $1 without any fees.
This existing habit helped them establish extensive markets that a new entrant cannot replicate overnight.
However, OUSD is starting within the financial systems that handle payments directly, leveraging card networks and Shopify stores, where USDT and USDC have minimal influence.
This market includes many of the 35% of Americans who now own cryptocurrency.
As Open Standard CEO Zach Abrams explains, "Every other stablecoin is building a fund.
For XRP holders (CRYPTO:XRP), the fate of RLUSD primarily relates to Ripple's business developments and does not directly influence XRP’s value.

Ripple sells RLUSD to banks and payment institutions for cross-border transactions, just the type of customers that OUSD’s partners are already accommodating.
With OUSD backed by major players like Visa and Mastercard, institutions assessing payment networks will have to consider this strong competitor.
Among established tokens, USDC faces the biggest risk from Open USD.
Circle already splits reserve income with its distributors, and since Coinbase benefits from USDC revenue and is also an OUSD partner, it can promote whichever token offers them more profit.
Unlike Tether and Circle, which issue USDC and keep most of the interest income from their reserves, OUSD shares most of that revenue with its partners.
These partners receive earnings based on their participation, and they can create and redeem tokens at $1 without any fees.
This existing habit helped them establish extensive markets that a new entrant cannot replicate overnight.
However, OUSD is starting within the financial systems that handle payments directly, leveraging card networks and Shopify stores, where USDT and USDC have minimal influence.
This market includes many of the 35% of Americans who now own cryptocurrency.
As Open Standard CEO Zach Abrams explains, "Every other stablecoin is building a fund.
For XRP holders (CRYPTO:XRP), the fate of RLUSD primarily relates to Ripple's business developments and does not directly influence XRP’s value.
